power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Sample size adequacy for the confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was considered using both previous simulation-based recommendations and a formal model-based power analysis. CFA models with moderate factor loadings (.50-.70) and at least three items per factor generally require samples of about 300-400 participants to achieve good statistical power (Wolf et al., 2013). In the previous ASA validation study the weakest standardized factor loading was approximately .64, indicating moderately strong item-factor relationships. In addition, a power analysis was conducted using semPower (Moshagen & Bader, 2024). For the specified 14item, three-factor CFA model (df = 74), assuming α = .05, power = .80, and an RMSEA of .05 as the degree of model misspecification to be detected, approximately 194 participants were required. The available CFA sample of 1,199 participants therefore substantially exceeded both the model-based requirement and previous simulation-based recommendations.

text.text: Anhedonia is a core symptom of depression linked to poorer outcomes in young people.
The Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) is a 14-item multidimensional measure validated in 11-18-year-olds.
We examined its psychometric properties in 1,199 individuals aged 16-25 years, with and without clinical diagnoses.
Confirmatory factor analysis supported the original three-factor structure over one-and two-factor alternatives.

Internal consistency was excellent for the total scale (α = .92), acceptable to good for the subscales (α = .71-.88) and comparable across age and clinical groups; five-month test-retest reliability was moderate (ICC = .69).

The ASA correlated with the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (SHAPS; r = .66) and ₛ depressive symptoms (r = .80), explained variance in depressive symptoms beyond the ₛ SHAPS (ΔR² = .32), and predicted depressive symptoms five months later beyond baseline symptoms.
The ASA is a reliable, valid measure of anhedonia across adolescence and young adulthood.
Anhedonia, defined as a reduced capacity to experience pleasure, is a core symptom of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2013).

It is highly prevalent among young people with depression, affecting approximately 50-78% (Malhi & Mann, 2018), and is associated with greater illness severity and poorer outcomes (Gabbay et al., 2015).

text.text: Despite its clinical importance, relatively few measures of anhedonia have been developed specifically to reflect how it is experienced and expressed by young people and existing measures do not always capture the multidimensional nature of anhedonia (Ma et al., 2026).

text.text: As the ASA was originally developed and validated in adolescents aged 11-18 years, it remains unclear whether its psychometric properties extend into young adulthood.

This is important because the transition from adolescence to young adulthood is accompanied by substantial developmental, social, and functional changes, and the experience and expression of anhedonia may vary across this period (Ma et al., 2026).

text.text: A measure developed specifically from adolescents' experiences cannot necessarily be assumed to retain the same factor structure, reliability, and validity as individuals transition into young adulthood.
Establishing whether the psychometric properties of the ASA extend across this developmental period is therefore important for determining its applicability to a broader age range.
It is also important to establish whether the ASA performs consistently across individuals with and without clinical diagnoses.
Anhedonia is particularly relevant to depression, but considerable variation exists in its severity and presentation.

Individuals with a clinical diagnosis may differ from those without a diagnosis in symptom severity, functional impairment, and experiences of anhedonia, which could influence the performance and interpretation of the measure.
Examining the ASA across clinical and non-clinical groups is therefore important for determining its broader research and clinical utility.

The present study aimed to extend the validation of the ASA into young adulthood using a large sample of older adolescents and young adults aged 16-25 years, including individuals with and without clinical diagnoses.

We examined whether the original three-factor structure of the ASA was supported in this broader age range and assessed the internal consistency and test-retest reliability of the total scale and its subscales.

Convergent validity was examined in relation to the Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale (Snaith et al., 1995), and concurrent validity was examined in relation to depressive symptoms measured using the Mood and Feelings Questionnaire (Angold et al., 1987).

text.text: We additionally examined whether ASA scores and psychometric properties were comparable across older adolescents and young adults and across clinical and non-clinical groups.
Finally, we examined the predictive validity of the ASA over time, including its ability to predict subsequent depressive symptoms.
Together, these analyses provide a comprehensive evaluation of whether the psychometric properties and utility of the ASA extend from adolescence into young adulthood.

The Mood and Feeling Questionnaire (MFQ)
The MFQ is a self-report questionnaire commonly used to screen for depressive symptoms in children and adolescents (Jarbin et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The MFQ is a self-report questionnaire commonly used to screen for depressive symptoms in children and adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Jarbin et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: It consists of 33 items rated on a three-point scale (0 = not true,1 = sometimes,2 = true), with higher scores indicating higher levels of depression and is one-dimensional.
Scores range from 0 to 66.

Previous research has reported excellent internal consistency for MFQ scores (Cronbach's alpha .91 to .93), together with evidence of validity and reasonable diagnostic accuracy, with a suggested clinical depression cut-off score of 27 (Thabrew et al., 2018).

text.text: The SHAPS is a self-report tool designed to assess hedonic capacity, or the ability to experience pleasure (Snaith et al., 1995).
text.formatted: The SHAPS is a self-report tool designed to assess hedonic capacity, or the ability to experience pleasure <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Snaith et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: It comprises 14 items, each rated on a four-point scale, covering various aspects of pleasurable experiences in four domains: interest/pastimes, social interaction, sensory experience, and food/drink.
Previous research has reported good internal consistency for SHAPS scores (Cronbach's α = .86) (Snaith et al., 1995).
text.formatted: Previous research has reported good internal consistency for SHAPS scores (Cronbach's α = .86) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Snaith et al., 1995)</ref>.

text.text: Originally, it was scored using a dichotomous system with a total score ranging from 0 to 14.
However, a four-point Likert scale has been suggested to better distinguish levels of severity for each item (Franken et al., 2007).

text.text: In the present study, items were scored 1-4 (total range 14-56), with higher scores indicating greater anhedonia.
A recent study with a non-clinical student sample identified a cut-off score of 23.5 for the nonclinical group (Ho et al., 2024).

text.text: The ASA was created in collaboration with adolescents experiencing symptoms of depression and anhedonia (Watson et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The ASA was created in collaboration with adolescents experiencing symptoms of depression and anhedonia <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Watson et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Informed by qualitative interviews, the ASA is a multidimensional self-report questionnaire designed to measure anhedonia in adolescents aged 11-18 years.
It covers various components of the anhedonia experience relevant to this age group.
The scale consists of 14 items rated on a four-point scale (0 = never,1 = sometimes,2 = often,3 = always), with higher scores indicating higher levels of anhedonia.
Total scores range from 0 to 42.
The ASA comprises three subscales:  ASA S1-Enjoyment, Excitement, and Emotional Flattening: It has 7 items in the scale and can range from 0 to 21.
 ASA S2-Enthusiasm, Connection, and Purpose: has 3 positively worded items, with scores ranging from 0 to 9.
Items were reverse scored for analysis so that, consistent with the other ASA subscales and the total score, higher scores indicate greater anhedonia.
 ASA S3-Effort, Motivation, and Drive: It has 4 items in the scale and can range from 0 to 12 (see Supplement for scale details).

In the original validation samples, ASA scores demonstrated excellent internal consistency, with α = .93-.94 for the total score and α values ranging from acceptable to excellent .79 to .92 for the subscales.
Test-retest reliability of ASA scores was moderate in the original validation sample (ICC = 0.73).
The scale encompasses both consummatory (enjoyment in the moment) and anticipatory (looking forward to future pleasures) aspects of anhedonia, as well as motivational deficits.
This multidimensional approach provides a more comprehensive assessment of anhedonia in adolescents compared to the SHAPS.

text.text: Participant demographics were summarized using descriptive statistics, and associations between questionnaire measures were examined using Spearman's rank correlation analysis.
Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) was conducted to assess the effects of clinical diagnosis, medication status, and age group on the three ASA subscale scores (ASA 1, ASA 2, and ASA 3).
ASA total scores were analysed separately using factorial ANOVA.
The analyses included all main effects, two-way interactions, and the three-way interaction.
MANOVA results were followed by univariate ANOVAs.
Multivariate effects were evaluated using Pillai's trace, and partial eta-squared (ηp²) was reported for univariate effects.
The analyses included 456 participants with complete information on diagnosis, medication status, and age group.
Given the unequal subgroup sizes, interaction effects were additionally examined using heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors and stratified bootstrap sensitivity analyses (2000 samples).

Group comparisons were made to examine the reliability and validity findings between two age groups, 16-19 (older adolescents) and 20-25 (young adults), and between clinical and non-clinical participants.
The classification of clinical versus non-clinical was determined by participants' self-reports on whether they had received a clinical diagnosis of depression.
We checked the normality of the data using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests to guide the selection of appropriate statistical methods.

The majority of the total sample and all subsamples, except for the follow-up subsample of 332 participants, had p-values less than 0.05 on these tests, indicating non normally distributed ASA scores.
For variables or subsamples that violated the normality assumption, non-parametric alternatives were employed, or bootstrapping with 2000 samples was applied to ensure robust and reliable results.
Internal consistency of the ASA total and its subscale scores was assessed using Cronbach's alpha.

Internal consistency values were interpreted as follows: values above 0.70 indicate acceptable reliability, values above 0.80 indicate good reliability, and values above 0.90 indicate excellent reliability.

Corrected item-total correlations were examined to assess the extent to which individual items were associated with the overall scale by calculating Spearman's rank correlation coefficients at both Time 1 and Time 2 between each item and the total ASA score (excluding the item in question).
A threshold of 0.40 was used to assess whether each item sufficiently contributed to the overall construct (Vaske et al., 2017).

text.text: We also conducted Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) in AMOS to validate the three-factor structure of ASA.
We compared the three-factor structure to a one-factor solution to evaluate whether the original three-factor model provided a better representation of the underlying constructs.
As an additional robustness check, one-, two-, and three-factor CFA models were compared using robust maximum likelihood estimation (MLR) in R with the lavaan package (version 0.7-2).
The alternative two-factor model combined ASA 1 and ASA 3 while retaining ASA 2 as a separate factor.
Model fit was assessed using robust fit indices (CFI, TLI, RMSEA), SRMR, and the Akaike and Bayesian information criteria (AIC and BIC).
Model-based reliability was estimated using McDonald's omega, from the correlated three-factor CFA model using MLR, computed with semTools (Jorgensen et al., 2022).

text.text: Incremental and predictive validity were examined using cross-sectional and longitudinal analyses, respectively.

Incremental validity was assessed by examining whether ASA T1 scores explained additional variance in MFQ T1 scores beyond SHAPS T1 scores using hierarchical multiple regression analyses, with SHAPS entered in the first step and ASA in the second, in the subsample with available SHAPS data (n = 433).
Longitudinal predictive validity was examined by assessing associations between ASA and MFQ scores across Time 1 and Time 2.
Spearman's rank correlation coefficients were used to evaluate these relationships, with higher correlations indicating stronger predictive validity.

Multiple regression analyses were conducted to examine whether baseline ASA scores predicted MFQ T2 scores after accounting for baseline MFQ scores, and whether baseline MFQ scores predicted ASA T2 scores after accounting for baseline ASA scores.
Collinearity diagnostics were performed, and Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) values were examined to ensure that multicollinearity was within the acceptable range (VIF = 1 to 5).
Regression models were run with and without controlling for age group, medication status, and depression diagnosis.
However, for the longitudinal model, only age group could be controlled due to limitations in the availability of other variables for this subsample.
Baseline characteristics of participants who did and did not complete follow-up were compared using Mann-Whitney U tests, chi-square tests and logistic regression.
We first performed a missing value analysis before the main analyses.
Of all item responses, there were 103 missing values (0.26%) for MFQ T1, 25 (0.23%) for MFQ T2, 12 (0.07%) for ASA T1, and 7 (0.15%) for ASA T2.

Given the low proportion of missing responses, missing items at both time points were replaced during data preprocessing using participant-level mean scores, rounded to the nearest valid response category.
A complete-case sensitivity analysis was also conducted for the longitudinal regression models (n = 312).
The total sample (N = 1199) consisted of 49% individuals aged 16-19 and 51% aged 20-25 (M age = 20; SD = 2.5).
The gender distribution was 72.8% female (n = 873), 23.9% male (n = 287), 2.9% another gender (n = 35), and 0.3% preferred not to say (n = 4).

Participants identified as White (61.2%), Asian or Asian British (16.2%), mixed or multiple ethnic groups (6.3%), Black or Black British (3.6%), or another ethnic group (5.2%, including Arab and Hispanic/Latino); a further 7.0% selected the combined category "Black, Asian and Minority Ethnic", and 0.5% did not report their ethnicity.

The present study extended the validation of the Anhedonia Scale for Adolescents (ASA) from adolescence into young adulthood, examining its psychometric properties in a large sample of individuals aged 16-25 years with varying levels of depressive symptoms and with and without clinical diagnoses.
Overall, the findings provide support for the reliability, factor structure, convergent and concurrent validity, and temporal stability of the ASA in this broader age range.

The original three-factor structure was supported and provided a better fit to the data than both one-and two-factor alternatives in the additional robust CFA analyses, while reliability estimates were broadly comparable across older adolescents and young adults.
The ASA was also strongly associated with established measures of anhedonia and depressive symptoms and demonstrated moderate test-retest reliability over time.

Importantly, longitudinal analyses indicated that ASA scores predicted subsequent depressive symptoms, even after accounting for baseline depressive symptoms, providing evidence that the measure may capture clinically meaningful aspects of anhedonia that are relevant to later depression.
The CFA provided support for the original three-factor structure of the ASA in older adolescents and young adults.

The three-factor model demonstrated reasonable overall fit and performed better than the alternative one-factor model, with additional robust CFA analyses also showing a modest improvement in fit over the alternative two-factor model, supporting the multidimensional conceptualisation of anhedonia underlying the original ASA (Watson et al., 2021).

Internal consistency provided further support for the reliability of the ASA in older adolescents and young adults.
Reliability was excellent for the total scale and ranged from acceptable to good across the three subscales.
This indicates strong internal consistency for the overall ASA.

Importantly, internal consistency was broadly comparable across age groups and across participants with and without a clinical diagnosis, suggesting that the ASA performs reliably across the developmental and clinical groups examined.
Consistent with the original validation study, the Enthusiasm, Connection, and Purpose subscale (ASA 2) showed lower internal consistency than the other two subscales.

The ASA demonstrated adequate temporal stability across the approximately five-month follow-up period.
Test-retest reliability was moderate for the total scale (ICC = .69) and across the three subscales (ICCs = .52-.66), indicating that the ASA provides reasonably stable measurement over time.
This extends the test-retest reliability reported in the original adolescent validation and provides further evidence that the measure remains reliable into young adulthood.
Similar temporal reliability estimates across the two age groups also support its use across the transition from later adolescence into young adulthood.
Convergent validity was supported by significant associations between the ASA and the SHAPS, an established measure of anhedonia.

The association was strongest for the total ASA and the Enjoyment, Excitement, and Emotional Flattening subscale, while associations were weaker for Enthusiasm, Connection, and Purpose and Effort, Motivation, and Drive.

This pattern is theoretically plausible given that the SHAPS primarily assesses hedonic capacity and pleasurable experiences, whereas the ASA was developed to capture a broader, multidimensional experience of anhedonia that additionally includes motivation, effort, connection and purpose.
The measures would therefore be expected to overlap substantially without being interchangeable.
Consistent with this interpretation, participants classified as experiencing higher anhedonia according to the SHAPS also had substantially higher ASA scores.
The interaction involving effort, motivation and drive is also noteworthy.
Participants with a clinical diagnosis of depression who were taking medication and were aged 16-19 reported particularly high levels of effort-related anhedonia.
This may suggest that motivational aspects of anhedonia are particularly pronounced in some younger individuals with more clinically significant presentations.
However, these findings were not consistently supported by additional analyses and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.
Replication in larger clinical samples is required before drawing conclusions about developmental or medication-related differences in effort-related anhedonia.
An important extension of the original ASA validation was the examination of predictive validity over time.
Baseline ASA scores were strongly associated with subsequent ASA scores and significantly predicted depressive symptoms approximately five months later.
Moreover, baseline ASA remained a significant predictor of subsequent depressive symptoms when baseline depression was included in the model.
This suggests that the ASA may capture information relevant to the subsequent course of depressive symptoms rather than simply reflecting concurrent depression severity.
The comparison with the SHAPS provides additional evidence for the potential utility of the ASA.
Cross-sectionally, the ASA explained a substantial proportion of variance in depressive symptoms beyond the SHAPS (32%), whereas the SHAPS added less than 1% beyond the ASA.

This broadly corresponds with findings from the original validation study, in which the ASA showed stronger associations with depression severity than existing measures of anhedonia (Watson et al., 2021).

text.text: One possible explanation is the ASA's broader assessment of anhedonia.

By incorporating enjoyment and emotional flattening alongside enthusiasm, connection, purpose, effort, motivation and drive, the ASA may capture aspects of anhedonia that are particularly relevant to depressive symptomatology but are less comprehensively represented by measures focused predominantly on hedonic capacity.
The longitudinal findings also suggest associations between anhedonia and depressive symptoms over time in both directions.
Baseline ASA scores predicted subsequent MFQ scores after accounting for baseline MFQ scores, while baseline MFQ scores also predicted subsequent ASA scores after accounting for baseline ASA scores.

At the subscale level, Enjoyment, Excitement, and Emotional Flattening and Effort, Motivation, and Drive were associated with subsequent depressive symptoms in the primary regression model, whereas Enthusiasm, Connection, and Purpose did not.

Although these findings should not be interpreted as demonstrating causality, they suggest that particular dimensions of anhedonia may be especially relevant to the persistence or development of depressive symptoms.
Further longitudinal research with multiple assessment points will be important for establishing the temporal relationship between specific dimensions of anhedonia and depression.
Several strengths of the present study should be noted.
First, the large sample enabled evaluation of the ASA across a broader developmental range than the original validation and provided substantial power for examination of its factor structure.

Second, the study evaluated multiple aspects of psychometric performance, including internal consistency, factor structure, test-retest reliability, convergent and concurrent validity, and longitudinal predictive validity.

The inclusion of both older adolescents and young adults, as well as participants with and without clinical diagnoses, also allowed the performance of the ASA to be examined across populations with differing developmental and clinical characteristics.

Finally, the longitudinal component extends previous predominantly cross-sectional validation evidence and provides initial evidence that ASA scores are informative about subsequent depressive symptoms.
Several limitations should be noted.
The sample was predominantly female.
Clinical diagnoses were self-reported rather than verified by diagnostic interview and were available for only a subset of participants, with fewer diagnosed participants remaining at follow-up.

This limited separate longitudinal analyses in clinical and non-clinical groups, and attrition was selective: follow-up completers had higher baseline depressive and anhedonic symptoms and were more often female, so the longitudinal sample over-represents more symptomatic participants.

The SHAPS was not available at both time points for the full longitudinal sample, preventing direct comparison of the predictive performance of the ASA and SHAPS; repeated measurement of both would clarify their relative sensitivity to change.

Although the three-factor model was supported, discriminant validity between factors was mixed and ASA-2 performed less well than the other subscales, so further work should examine whether items could be refined while preserving the multidimensional content of the original measure.

Finally, although reliability estimates were similar across age groups, further research is needed to establish whether ASA scores can be interpreted equivalently across developmental and clinical groups.
The present findings extend the validation of the ASA beyond the adolescent age range in which it was originally developed and provide evidence for its use in older adolescents and young adults.

The original three-factor structure was supported, the total scale demonstrated excellent internal consistency and moderate test-retest reliability, and the ASA showed convergent validity with an established measure of anhedonia and strong concurrent associations with depressive symptoms.

Importantly, baseline ASA scores also predicted subsequent depressive symptoms, suggesting that the measure may have value for identifying dimensions of anhedonia relevant to the course of depression.

Taken together, these findings support the ASA as a reliable and valid multidimensional measure of anhedonia across the transition from adolescence into young adulthood, while highlighting the need for further investigation of the distinction between its component dimensions and its performance in independently characterised clinical samples.

text.text: The strong association between ASA and MFQ scores provides evidence of concurrent validity and is consistent with the central role of anhedonia in depression.

Participants with higher levels of depressive symptoms had substantially higher ASA scores, and participants reporting a clinical diagnosis of depression also showed greater overall anhedonia, particularly in enjoyment/emotional flattening and effort/motivation.
These findings indicate that the ASA is sensitive to depression-relevant variation in symptom severity.

This is consistent with recent evidence that the Chinese ASA distinguishes adolescents with MDD and subthreshold depression from healthy controls, with ROC-derived cut-offs of 21.5 and 15.5, respectively (Kuan et al., 2026), and that a cut-off of 20.5 identifies adolescents with marked anhedonia (Ye et al., 2025).

text.text: At the same time, anhedonia and depression should not be regarded as equivalent constructs.
The strong association between ASA and MFQ scores is expected given that anhedonia is a core feature of depression, but the magnitude of this relationship also warrants consideration.

The ASA was specifically designed to provide a detailed assessment of anhedonic experiences, including motivational and affective components that are not comprehensively assessed by general depression measures.

Future work should therefore examine the extent to which ASA scores provide clinically useful information beyond overall depression severity, including their relationships with functioning, prognosis and treatment response.
No overall effect of age group was observed for ASA total or subscale scores.
This finding suggests that, within the 16-25-year age range examined here, chronological age alone may not be strongly associated with the severity of anhedonia.
In contrast, clinical diagnosis was associated with higher ASA scores.
Together with the comparable reliability estimates across age groups, these findings support the applicability of the ASA beyond the adolescent population in which it was originally developed.
